description:
See You é uma equipe que, assim como sua mascote, a foca astronauta de binóculos, observa o mundo para encontrar o que o espaço ainda não mostrou. O nome é um jogo de palavras com Seal (foca) e carrega duas ideias: “see”, ver e identificar, e “you”, as pessoas e o planeta que a gente quer entender melhor.

Nosso desafio é encontrar na Terra os lugares mais parecidos com as futuras bases na Lua e em Marte, para preparar a exploração espacial de forma mais segura e acessível.
summary: See You is an interactive 3D globe of Earth, the Moon and Mars that finds places on Earth resembling candidate permanent Moon base sites and key Mars locations. Click any point on Earth and it scores, with real NASA and ESA satellite data, how similar that place is to six lunar and Martian targets, explains why it matches and why it doesn’t, and shows what Earth can never reproduce. It turns analog site selection, usually based on tradition and expert intuition, into a transparent, data-driven and verifiable process.
details:
What exactly does it do and how does it work?
See You is a data analysis tool built around a 3D globe of three bodies: Earth, the Moon and Mars. The user picks one of six targets:

  • Moon: the Shackleton–de Gerlache ridge (Artemis candidate region), Cabeus crater (permanently shadowed, with water ice) and Mare Tranquillitatis.
  • Mars: Jezero crater, Gale crater and Arcadia Planitia (shallow ground ice, candidate human landing site).

The investigation then follows four steps:

  1. Target: choose a site on the Moon or Mars and press “See analogs on Earth”.
  2. Explore: click anywhere on Earth, or browse the similarity heat map and the “Top Locations” ranking.
  3. Compare: the panel shows the overall score and a breakdown by dimension: relief, thermal, surface, water and operations.
  4. Explain: every result comes with “Why?”, “Why not?” and a fixed line of what Earth never reproduces (gravity, vacuum or thin atmosphere, radiation).

Under the hood, an offline Python pipeline downloads real data and builds a global 0.25° land grid (~16 MB) with eight parameters:

  • slope and roughness, from the Copernicus DEM GLO-90;
  • day–night temperature range and minimum temperature, from MODIS LST;
  • NDVI and albedo, from MODIS;
  • annual rainfall, from GPM IMERG;
  • ground ice, from MODIS snow cover and ESA CCI Permafrost.

The same parameters are measured on the targets. Topography comes from cut-outs of LOLA and MOLA. The other target values (temperatures from Diviner, REMS and MEDA, ice evidence from LEND and SHARAD, albedo from TES) are published values from peer-reviewed papers, cited with their DOI.

Each parameter is scored from 0 to 1:

  • two-sided parameters use s = exp(−((Earth − target)/σ)²);
  • parameters whose target is zero (rainfall, NDVI) use s = exp(−Earth/σ);
  • categorical parameters (illumination, ground ice) use lookup tables.

Missing data is shown as N/A and never counted as zero.

What benefits does it offer?
It replaces “this place feels like Mars” with a measurable, reproducible answer. Researchers, mission planners, educators and students can check known analogs against the data, compare candidate sites side by side, and see exactly which conditions match and which fail. Every number in the interface states the instrument and the product it came from.

What is the intended impact of the project?
Analog sites are where astronauts train and where rovers, habitats and resource technologies are tested before going to the Moon and Mars. We want to make analog selection more transparent and to widen the search beyond the classic sites, especially in under-studied regions such as South America. Our highlighted discovery is the Araguainha impact crater in Brazil, the largest impact structure in South America and rarely used as an analog.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Front end: React 18, TypeScript and Vite, with a 3D globe built on react-globe.gl and three.js. Imagery comes from NASA GIBS (Blue Marble, MODIS NDVI, MODIS LST), Moon Trek (LRO WAC) and Mars Trek (Viking MDIM 2.1).
  • Data pipeline: Python 3.12 managed with uv, using earthaccess, xarray, rioxarray, rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, pandas, h5py, h5netcdf and pyhdf. Tests use pytest with synthetic data.
  • Architecture: serverless. Data is processed once and served as static files, so the demo is fast, free to host and does not depend on a login or an API at runtime.
  • Design: Figma. The interface is in Portuguese and English.

What is the creative aspect of your project?
The map is only the showcase. The product is the explainable comparison panel. Instead of a single “black box” score, the tool shows where an analogy works and, just as clearly, where it breaks. For example, the thermal dimension always scores low for the lunar poles (around −230 °C in shadowed craters). The tool is also built for discovery, not only to confirm known analogs: the same metric that ranks the Atacama for Mars can surface overlooked places like Araguainha.

What factors did your team consider?
We prioritized scientific honesty and traceability:

  • Same scale and units: all three bodies use the same ~2 km horizontal scale and the same units.
  • Stated limits: we say openly that there is no official NASA standard for analog parameters. The variables come from NASA and ESA data products, and the tolerances (σ) and weights are our documented choices, editable in a single configuration file.
  • Confidence labels: every target value carries a confidence level (computed, derived, estimate or published) and a citation.
  • Validation: the pipeline checks physical ranges and data coverage, and blocks the export if values are out of range.
  • Role of AI: an AI assistant helped write code and documentation, but every score is calculated deterministically from the data.
  • Reliability: we chose static hosting so the demo cannot go down during judging.
